newsitem.title: USA: No suggestion of "hush money" for Hubbell-McCurry.
newsitem.headline: No suggestion of "hush money" for Hubbell-McCurry.

text.p: White House aides Erskine Bowles and Mack McLarty would never have tried to find work for former Associate Attorney General Webster Hubbell if they had known he would plead guilty to two felony counts later the same year, White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Saturday.
McCurry told CNN's "Capital Gang" programme the two men were simply trying to help Hubbell find work to support his family.
White House Chief of Staff Erskine Bowles received a subpoena on Friday to appear before the Whitewater grand jury to answer questions about his efforts on Hubbell's behalf.

"If either one of them had known that by the end of that year Web Hubbell was going to plead guilty to two felonies they wouldn't have gone and stuck their necks out and tried to help him," McCurry said.

Hubbell resigned from the Justice Department in 1994 and was sent to jail in 1995 after he pleaded guilty to fraudulent billing of clients at the Rose law firm of Little Rock, Arkansas, before he joined the Clinton administration. He and first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton were partners at the firm.

He received payments from the Riady family of Indonesia, which has close ties to President Bill Clinton, for work on a project in China after he resigned. The White House said none of the calls made on Hubbell's behalf involved Lippo, an Indonesian conglomerate run by the Riady family.

The former Clinton associate also got payments from others with ties to Clinton, leading critics to ask if the payments were "hush money" to keep him from telling what he knew about the Whitewater case, a tangled web of financial, legal and ethical questions that have dogged Clinton and his wife since Clinton's 1992 campaign for the presidency.
McCurry said there was never any suggestion that "hush money" should have been paid.

"If there had been any suggestion that hush money should have been paid... I know both of them (Bowles and McLarty) well enough to know what they would have done ... they have gone to the U.S. attorney," he said.
Hubbell denied he was withholding information that would be damaging to the president and his wife.

Clinton on Thursday said he did not think the two men's actions were wrong and said that at the time "no one had any idea what the nature of the allegations was against Mr. Hubbell or whether they were true."

Republican Senator Mitch McConnell of Kentucky said he was glad an independent counsel was investigating the Hubbell matter, but urged Attorney General Janet Reno to appoint a second independent counsel to investigate allegations of illegal fund raising by Clinton and the Democrats as well.
The White House last week released more papers belonging to former aide Harold Ickes which documented intense pressure on Clinton to raise money for his 1996 re-election campaign.

The 6-inch-high stack of more than 2,000 pages showed that party officials pressed Clinton, Vice President Al Gore and first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton to call donors directly, a practice the president dislikes and cannot recall doing.

They also showed the White House, while consistently denying it solicited donors at more than 100 coffees held at the White House, which would be illegal, typically set and reached $400,000 fund-raising targets for the events.
McConnell, who heads the Senate Republican's campaign fund-raising committee, said he had no problem with Clinton's involvement in his party's political work.
"What I don't like and what appears to be a violation of the law is use of federal property for that purpose," McConnell told CNN's "Inside Politics Weekend."
